abstract: Higher-order body representations, including representations of body shape and size, play an important role in maintaining perceptual constancy in touch. However, whether the development of these representations depends on early visual experience remains unclear. Here, we investigated tactile distance perception in congenitally blind, late-blind, and sighted individuals. A given tactile distance is typically perceived as longer on the finger than on the forearm, reflecting distortions in cortical topography that is partially rescaled by higher-order representations of body size and shape. Congenitally blind participants showed a greater tendency to perceive identical tactile distances on the index finger as longer than those on the forearm. A similar bias was observed when comparing the forehead and face, suggesting that altered tactile distance perception in congenital blindness is not limited to body regions with extensive sensory-motor experience. Furthermore, within the late-blind group, the similarity of perceptual patterns to sighted controls, relative to congenitally blind participants, was associated with blindness duration. Together, these findings suggest that both early visual and post-blindness experience contributes to the calibration of tactile distance perception across the body, with its influence potentially extending beyond body regions extensively engaged in sensory-motor activities.
